extracted.intended_audience: local government managers, staff, and public servants (city/county administrators, assistants, department heads, communications staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for communicating effectively with staff, elected officials, and residents in local government settings, covering fundamentals (why) and actionable techniques (how) for in-person and digital interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past, present, and future context
rubrics_metrics.description: When we communicate with anyone, that event has a past, a present, and a future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that recipients bring prior experiences (past) that shape how they hear you now (present) and that each interaction influences future communications. Be clear, fair, judicious, and kind because you don't know people's histories and interactions can have outsized downstream effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation in communication is continuous and simultaneous
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot not communicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat silence, ignoring messages, social media history, and non-responses as forms of communication. Understand that actions like ghosting, not replying, or old posts are still sending signals; manage your online presence and expectations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and negotiate roles people play
rubrics_metrics.description: People bring different roles (e.g., citizen/homeowner, professional, friend) into conversations and may shift roles depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask questions to clarify purpose (e.g., 'What is your purpose today?'), be aware of role-switching, and adapt your approach depending on whether someone is acting as a complainant, information-seeker, advocate, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start by finding common ground and personal connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the person to tell you about themselves; find shared connections or mutual acquaintances to diffuse tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social media and prior knowledge to identify commonalities (e.g., 'Do you know Tom Knight?'). Personal connections often diffuse anger and build rapport quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy: listen to understand, not to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to see the situation through the other person's eyes and validate emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge emotions explicitly (e.g., 'You're really upset today') and offer to help. Empathy is especially crucial in public service where distrust or prior negative experiences may predispose skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active listening and paraphrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Active listening is not passive; it involves paraphrasing and confirming understanding so the speaker feels heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen to understand, not to rebut. Paraphrase without interrupting and invite correction ('Is that what you mean?'). This reduces misunderstandings and defuses conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOLER nonverbal technique (Square off, Open up, Lean in, Eye contact, Relax)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five nonverbal behaviors that signal attention and presence: square off, open up, lean in, eye contact, relax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SOLER to communicate availability and engagement: turn shoulder-to-shoulder (square off), avoid crossed arms (open up), lean in slightly when they speak, maintain appropriate eye contact (camera in virtual settings), and relax your posture. Apply in-person and adapt for digital (look at the camera).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonverbal communication weight and congruence
rubrics_metrics.description: A large portion of meaning is carried nonverbally (estimated range 67–93%, commonly referenced as ~80%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your nonverbal signals align with your words. Mixed messages (nonverbal saying one thing while words say another) damage trust more than consistent communication. Practice to make nonverbal and verbal messages congruent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up and continuing the communication event
rubrics_metrics.description: No communication event is truly over; follow-up shows you value the interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use timely, personalized follow-up (postcards, individualized emails, phone calls) to show commitment and to close loops. Follow through on promises and schedule callbacks; failure to deliver undermines integrity and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalized responses over automated generic replies
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated 'do not reply' messages make residents feel unseen; individualized replies build trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, respond to constituents individually, name them, explain misunderstandings, and provide specifics. Even high-volume situations can be managed by distributing work across staff or using leadership mandates to prioritize personalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor communication style, frequency, and method to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt how you speak (direct vs. relational), how much detail you provide, and the medium based on the listener's preferences and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be authentic but flexible: be consistent publicly and in small groups, then adjust tone/length based on cues. Ask 'short story or long story?' or offer a one-paragraph summary with an invitation to dive deeper for those who want more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personality/people-mapping to customize approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tools (e.g., 'people map' with types: leader, people, free spirit, task) to understand how individuals prefer to receive information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify major/minor personality types to decide whether to lead with tasks or relational talk, and adapt phrasing and pacing accordingly. Use it as a team tool to set expectations and avoid misreading motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance conciseness and necessary detail (Aristotle's golden mean)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strike a middle ground between too terse (leaving out needed info) and too long (losing the audience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take cues from the recipient; offer a concise summary upfront and note that you can provide fuller details if desired. Label content as 'short story' vs 'long story' and let the recipient choose depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use silence strategically but avoid prolonged avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Silence can prevent rash responses (e.g., don't respond in anger), but prolonged silence (ghosting) communicates negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When angry, 'write it but don't send' and revisit later. Avoid letting issues fester; address tense interactions directly rather than leaving them unspoken. Use temporary silence to cool off, but follow up intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resetting tense professional relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: If interactions are repeatedly awkward or tense, explicitly ask for a reset or schedule a neutral meeting to clear the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say 'can we start over?' or suggest an off-site chat (coffee) to re-establish rapport. Use perception-checking language because the other person may not share your sense of tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set boundaries with chronic troublemakers and manage expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some participants seek to stir conflict; recognize when repeated engagement is unproductive and draw limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document prior outreach and proposed solutions, explain when further engagement is unlikely to be productive, or refer them to alternate channels. Protect staff time and mental health by setting clear boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Everyone shares responsibility for the success of public meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: All attendees (staff, commissioners, audience) influence a meeting's tone through verbal and nonverbal behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model respectful nonverbals (no phones, no rolling eyes, attentive posture). Leadership should set norms and expect participants to contribute constructively rather than merely pointing out problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-through and organizational commitment to communication practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Good communication practices (individual replies, follow-up) must be adopted across the organization or they overburden a few staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership should endorse and resource follow-up behaviors; distribute tasks (e.g., 400 individualized emails split among staff) to avoid burning out a single staff member. Consistent organizational commitment sustains trust-building efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be human: tell stories, be consistent, and be vulnerable to build trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity, personal stories, and consistency create connection with skeptical audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share brief personal anecdotes that illustrate values (why you care) and invite others to share theirs. Combine consistency in behavior with storytelling to overcome cynicism over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polite reminders for partial or missed email answers
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone answers part of a multi-question message but ignores others, assume oversight and prompt kindly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond with gratitude and a gentle nudge ('Thanks — could you please also respond to this item?'). If it's a boss, prioritize items they addressed and use completion as an opportunity to follow up on remaining items; maintain respect and professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abusing positional power; treat everyone with respect and equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if you represent leadership, do not wield authority as a blunt instrument; respect job roles and colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear when conveying directives from higher levels ('I'm asking on behalf of X'), but maintain respectful tone, avoid coercion, and ensure equitable treatment across departments.
